text: Three questions about the chapters, then the first step of your own writing. When a question asks for evidence, use Isaac's own words. In the Writer's Workshop you are only making a list today. Pick moments you can still feel.

Read Chapters 1 and 2 in your book. First, look at the old map. It was printed around the time of this story, and it shows where the Choctaw Nation was. Then do the quick check at the bottom of this tab.

This book starts with a boy who says something no narrator should be able to say. He is a ghost. Then he says he is not a ghost yet. Hold on to both of those. Today you meet Isaac, his family, and his dog Jumper, in the Choctaw Nation in 1830. Keep one question with you: what does Isaac know that you don't?

Two word parts run through this whole book. One is about remembering. One is about writing. Isaac is doing both. Try to find them before the page tells you. When you get to the river game, say each word slowly and listen for where your voice stops.
Three questions about Chapters 3 and 4, and then a draft of your own moment. Pick one moment from your list. Write it from the inside, with I, the way Isaac does.

Read Chapters 3 and 4 in your book. These are hard chapters. Isaac sees more visions, and then something happens that is not a vision at all. Take your time. When you finish, try the quick check, then the Read Like a Writer box.

Last lesson, Isaac saw something nobody else could see. Today you find out what it meant. Start with the warm-up. The DOL sentence comes straight from Chapter 4, and it moves. Then read the poem and listen for who is talking in it.
Today you match each word to its root, and you read this week's words in sentences from the book. In the river game, say each word slowly and listen for where your voice stops.
Three questions, and then you revise. Add one inside detail to your draft: something you saw, heard, felt, or thought. One detail can change a whole paragraph.
Read Chapters 5 and 6. The photo on this tab shows a real cypress swamp in Mississippi. Look at the color of the water. Then reread one passage, the way What Good Readers Do asks.
Isaac's family is in the swamp now, with almost nothing. Watch how the people work together. Start with the warm-up sentence about Old Man and his blanket.
Today you build appositives yourself and use your roots to work out words you have never seen. The river game has root stones now. Tap only the letters of the root.
Three questions, and the last one looks back over the whole week. Then write the clean, final version of your moment, and submit your work.
Read Chapter 7. Then look at the painting on this tab. When you finish, think about the whole week. What has Isaac's voice shown you that a history book could not?
This is the last day of the week, and Chapter 7 has a surprise in it. It is funny. Start with the warm-up. In the poem, think about the speaker, the voice inside the poem.
Last day with these roots. Build the words from their pieces, then use this week's words in your own sentences. Finish your river crossing too.

Read the opening of the book out loud. Isaac is talking right to you, so read it the way he would say it. Slow down on the warning at the end of the first paragraph. When it sounds smooth, record yourself and turn it in.
